title: “Only Murders in the Building” Season 6 Trailer Unveils “The Girl With the Curls” & British Brazzos
body:
The highly anticipated sixth season of Hulu’s comedy‑mystery “Only Murders in the Building” drops on Tuesday, December 8, and its first trailer promises a transatlantic twist, a new enigmatic guest star and a fresh batch of quirky clues that could finally shake up the beloved trio’s sleuthing formula. Featuring Steve Martin, Martin Short and Selena Gomez once again, the teaser reveals the cast stepping onto London’s fog‑laden streets, where a “girl with the curls” and a pair of British brazzos become central to the new case that will test the trio’s investigative chemistry.

The decision to relocate the action to the United Kingdom marks the series’ most ambitious setting shift to date. After three seasons anchored in the cramped, gossip‑laden corridors of New York’s Arconia, the move to London opens narrative doors to classic British mystery tropes—foggy alleys, aristocratic estates, and a tradition of eccentric detectives. Fans can expect the show’s signature blend of dry humor and meta‑commentary to riff on iconic British crime dramas, from “Sherlock” to “Midsomer Murders,” while still retaining its modern, self‑aware edge. The trailer’s quick cuts of double‑decker buses, red telephone boxes and rain‑slicked cobblestones hint at a visual style that will contrast sharply with the neon‑glow interiors of previous seasons.

At the heart of the new mystery is a character simply described as “the girl with the curls,” a figure who appears in the opening montage perched on a London balcony, her hair whipping in the wind as she watches the city below. Though her identity remains under wraps, early speculation points to a possible cameo by a prominent British actress known for both dramatic gravitas and comedic timing, a casting choice that could deepen the series’ cross‑cultural appeal. The “British brazzos” referenced in the trailer—a slang term for flamboyant, well‑dressed gentlemen—appear to be a duo of suspects or perhaps reluctant allies, adding a layer of class‑based intrigue that mirrors the show’s ongoing exploration of social status within the micro‑cosm of the Arconia.

The core trio—Martin’s eccentric, retired actor Charles, Short’s neurotic former TV host Oliver, and Gomez’s millennial podcaster Mabel—will have to adapt their investigative methods to a new environment. Their dynamic, built on a blend of generational perspectives and personal insecurities, has been the engine of the series’ success, and the London setting offers fresh challenges: navigating a city where privacy is a cultural norm, deciphering cryptic British slang, and contending with a police force that operates under different procedural constraints. Early teasers suggest that Charles will indulge in his love of classic British theater, Oliver will grapple with his unfamiliarity with the UK’s media landscape, and Momez will attempt to translate her podcasting skills to a new audience, possibly even launching a trans‑Atlantic true‑crime series of her own.

Beyond the narrative shifts, the season’s production values signal a significant budget increase. Filming on location in London, complete with authentic landmarks and period‑appropriate set pieces, underscores Hulu’s commitment to keeping the series fresh after five years on the air. The move also reflects a broader industry trend of American shows seeking global backdrops to attract international viewers and to capitalize on co‑production incentives. By embedding the story in a city with a storied detective heritage, “Only Murders” positions itself to tap into a worldwide fan base that appreciates both the comedy of its American roots and the gravitas of British mystery conventions.

As the countdown to December 8 begins, anticipation is high that the show will deliver both the comforting familiarity of its beloved cast and the exhilarating novelty of a new locale. If the trailer is any indication, the sixth season will push the series into uncharted territory while staying true to the witty, self‑referential tone that has made it a cultural touchstone. Viewers can look forward to a blend of humor, suspense and cross‑cultural commentary that could redefine the show’s legacy and set the stage for future seasons to explore even more global mysteries.
